title: Passover: the Song of Songs
hookLine: a love poem read at Passover, which the rabbis read as God and Israel
tomorrow: The Omer: one quality a day

lines: A LOVE POEM IN A HOLY BOOK.
cards: A love poem, of all things, in the Bible. Not a gentle one, either. Two lovers searching for each other through city streets at night.

Eyes like doves, hair like a flock of goats coming down a mountain. Kisses, perfume, a garden locked and then opened, a watchman in the streets. Nowhere in its eight chapters does God's name clearly appear.
And during the week of Passover, it's the custom in synagogue to read it aloud, beginning to end.

teach.b: It's called Shir HaShirim, the Song of Songs, meaning the greatest song, the way holy of holies means the holiest place. The rabbis of the Mishnah debated which books belonged in the Bible, and some doubted this one.
Rabbi Akiva answered: all the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies. He and the rabbis after him read it as a love song between God and the people Israel.
The ancient Aramaic translation, the Targum, goes further and reads it as Israel's history, starting with the Exodus. So why Passover? The plainest reason is the season.
In the old Jewish translation, the beloved calls: "For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone; the flowers appear on the earth; the time of singing is come."
Passover is the spring festival, and this is a spring poem. The deeper reason is the story.
In the rabbis' reading, the Exodus begins the romance: God takes Israel out of Egypt into the wilderness, like a bride following her beloved.
For some readers, one verse sums it up: "My beloved is mine, and I am his."
Among Ashkenazim, it's usually read on the Shabbat during the festival; some Sephardi communities also chant it every Friday evening, as Shabbat comes in. Read as a love poem, it's beautiful.
Read the rabbis' way, as a parable, it pictures the bond between God and Israel as longing, on both sides.

how: Many Ashkenazi synagogues read the Song of Songs aloud on the Shabbat during Passover, and some Sephardi and Mizrahi communities also chant it every Friday evening before Shabbat.

games.why: Akiva didn't just defend it. he ranked it highest: the holy of holies, a song between God and Israel.

practice: Find one line of love, from a poem, a letter you kept, a message someone once sent you, or one of today's verses, and read it slowly, twice.
Then sit with whoever it makes you think of: a partner, a parent, a child, a friend, or, if you pray, God. Let the longing in it be good rather than sad.
